intro: How your team saves, shares and reviews code: Git mechanics, how Bitbucket fits in, and the habits that separate smooth teams from messy ones.

1.summary: Repos, commits, branches, merges, and how Bitbucket fits in.

lesson.title: Git = save points for code
lesson.body:
**Git** is a tool that records the history of a project, like save points in a video game. You can always go back.

- A **repository** (**repo**) is a project folder that Git is tracking, including its full history.
- A **commit** is one save point: a snapshot of changes plus a short message explaining them ("Fix checkout button on mobile"). Each commit gets a unique ID (a **hash**) like `a1b2c3d`.

Git runs on your own computer. Nothing is shared until you choose to share it.
lesson.pm: Good commit messages are a free changelog. When something breaks, the history tells you what changed, when, and why.

lesson.title: Branches, and where Bitbucket fits
lesson.body:
A **branch** is a parallel line of work. You branch off `main` (the official version), make changes safely, and nothing on `main` is disturbed. When you're done, you **merge**: combine the branch's changes back into `main`.

**Bitbucket** (like GitHub or GitLab) is a website that hosts the team's shared copy of the repo, called the **remote**, plus team features like pull requests and pipelines. **Git is the tool; Bitbucket is the meeting place.**

- `git clone` downloads a copy of the repo
- `git pull` gets teammates' new commits
- `git push` uploads your commits
lesson.pm: When someone says a change is "on a branch," it isn't live and isn't in `main` yet. It's still in progress.

cards.back: A tool that records a project's history as save points (commits) and lets people work in parallel.
A project folder tracked by Git, including its whole history.
A save point: a snapshot of changes with a message explaining them.
A parallel line of work split off from `main`, so changes don't disturb the official version.
Combining one branch's changes into another (usually into `main`).
The shared copy of a repo hosted on a site like Bitbucket or GitHub.
Push uploads your commits to the remote. Pull downloads others' commits.

quiz.q: What's the relationship between Git and Bitbucket?
options: Git is the version-control tool; Bitbucket hosts shared repos and adds team features
They're competing tools; you use one or the other
quiz.why: Git does the tracking. Bitbucket (or GitHub/GitLab) hosts the remote and adds pull requests, pipelines, etc.

quiz.q: You finished work on your laptop. Which command shares your commits with the team?
quiz.why: Push sends your commits up to the remote.

quiz.q: Why work on a branch instead of directly on `main`?
options: So unfinished changes don't disturb the official version
Branches are free and main costs money
quiz.why: Branches isolate work in progress until it's reviewed and ready to merge.

quiz.q: Which is the best commit message?
options: "Fix checkout button not responding on iOS Safari"
quiz.why: A good message says what changed and ideally why. Future you will thank you.

options: Downloads a full copy of a remote repo to your computer
quiz.why: Clone gives you your own local copy of the repository to work in.

2.summary: Pull requests, merge conflicts, worktrees, rebase, and good vs bad habits.

lesson.title: Pull requests and merge conflicts
lesson.body:
A **pull request** (**PR**) is a formal ask: "please review my branch and merge it into main." On Bitbucket a PR shows the **diff** (what changed), lets teammates comment and **approve**, and runs **pipelines**: automated checks like tests and builds (configured in `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`).

A **merge conflict** happens when two branches changed *the same lines* differently. Git can't guess which version is right, so it stops and asks a human to choose. It's normal, not a disaster, but it's a sign that branches lived too long or overlapped.
lesson.pm: Small PRs get reviewed faster and more carefully. A 2,000-line PR usually gets a rubber stamp, and that's where bugs sneak through.

lesson.title: Worktrees, rebase, and good habits
lesson.body:
A **worktree** is a second working folder for the *same* repo, checked out to a different branch. You can have two branches open at once with no switching back and forth. It's great for running several Claude Code sessions on different tasks in parallel.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the latest `main`, for a cleaner, straight-line history. Because it rewrites history, **never rebase a branch others are using**. The same goes for `git push --force`, which overwrites the remote's history.

**Good habits:** small focused commits, clear messages, short-lived branches, pull `main` often, never commit secrets, and don't push straight to main.
**Bad habits:** "fix stuff" messages, giant PRs, branches that live for weeks, force-pushing shared branches.
lesson.pm: You can ask Claude Code to write the PR description for you. A good one explains *why*, *what changed* and *how it was tested*.

cards.back: A request to review a branch and merge it into main, with diff, comments, approvals and automated checks.
When two branches changed the same lines differently, so a human has to choose what's right.
Automated checks (tests, builds, deploys) that run on commits and PRs, defined in `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`.
An extra working folder for the same repo on a different branch, so you can work on two branches at once.
Replaying your commits on top of the latest main for a cleaner history. It rewrites history, so never do it on shared branches.
`git push --force`: overwrites the remote's history with yours. Dangerous on shared branches.

quiz.q: Git reports a merge conflict. What does that mean?
options: Two branches changed the same lines differently, and a person must decide
quiz.why: Conflicts are Git asking for a human decision. They're routine.

quiz.q: You want two Claude Code sessions working on two features at once without them tripping over each other. What helps?
quiz.why: Each worktree is its own folder on its own branch, so sessions don't overwrite each other's files.

options: Force-pushing to a branch teammates are also using
quiz.why: Force-pushing a shared branch overwrites others' history and can lose their work.

quiz.q: A PR's pipeline is red (failed). What should happen?
options: Merge anyway, since it's just a warning
quiz.why: Pipelines are the automated safety net. A red check usually means tests or the build broke.

quiz.q: Why do reviewers prefer small pull requests?
options: They're easier to review carefully, so bugs are more likely to be caught
quiz.why: Review quality drops sharply as PR size grows.
